frameworks.name: Rule of 100
frameworks.definition: A four-part daily framework: reach out to 100 people, create content requiring 100 minutes, spend $100+ on ads, and spend 100 minutes on ad creation and research.

frameworks.name: 13 Rules to Win at Anything
frameworks.definition: A structured set of 13 foundational principles for sustained success across business and personal endeavors, emphasizing instruction-following, persistence, skill development, pain-driven improvement, and long-term thinking.

claims.text: Follow instructions as the first principle of success; most people fail because they skip steps or deviate from proven processes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: The Rule of 100 (100 daily outreaches, 100 minutes of content, $100+ ad spend, 100 minutes on ad improvement) applied consistently yields exponential business growth; practitioners at day 60 report having more business than they can handle.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Consistent volume multiplies across outreach, content, and advertising, compounding across channels.
bounded_by: Requires sustained commitment; no single day's skip is acceptable

claims.text: Excitement fades after one week of starting any endeavor; this is the point where real work begins, not where it ends.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Initial emotional momentum wears off, revealing the grinding, repetitive nature of skill-building.

claims.text: Personal development through business (your own capability) compounds faster than the business output itself; you are the primary product being built.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Sustained business activity forces repeated decision-making, failure recovery, and skill acquisition, which accumulate into capability growth faster than revenue compounds.

claims.text: Everything is unscalable in the beginning; this is how you learn every piece of the business. Once you have learned each piece, people recognize you as an expert.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Unscalable work forces deep learning of every operational detail; this depth is the foundation of expertise recognition.

claims.text: Pain during repetitive work is the signal to lean into improvement, not to quit; avoiding pain prevents the discovery of better methods. The pain forces you to change, which builds skill.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Pain from repetition creates urgency to find more efficient or effective approaches; this urgency drives innovation and skill development.
bounded_by: Does not apply to harmful or destructive repetition

claims.text: Complaining is a net-zero to net-negative activity that wastes energy and destroys credibility; complainers are viewed as weak and powerless by observers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Thousands of people have already succeeded at any endeavor; if you do not succeed, it is because you are not yet skilled enough, not because the endeavor is impossible.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Before claiming a channel or method "doesn't work," reframe it as "I don't know how to make it work yet" or "I am not yet good enough."; channels generating billions in spend (e.g., Facebook ads, cold outbound) definitionally work, so your inability indicates a skill gap.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Shifting blame from external (channel failure) to internal (skill gap) enables problem-solving; it reframes failure as data about you, not the channel.

anchors.value: trillions of attempts daily across thousands of companies

bounded_by: Assumes you are attempting a method used at scale by others

claims.text: Business is shockingly simple (the rules are straightforward) but surprisingly hard (consistency and execution are brutal); the hard part is not insight but daily follow-through.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Simple rules are easy to understand but easy to skip; daily decisions to skip accumulate into failure.

claims.text: Suffering and hardship during the building phase fade from memory; people predominantly remember the success that followed, not the sacrifices that preceded it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Recency bias and narrative compression: fresher (current) memories overwrite distant (past) ones; success compounds continuously while hardship is episodic.

claims.text: Write down the reasons you will persist with a goal and revisit them during motivation dips; external reminders sustain conviction when internal motivation flags.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: during periods of low emotional motivation
claims.mechanism: Written reasons externalize conviction, creating an artifact that bypasses emotional fluctuations; revisiting them refreshes commitment without requiring new discoveries.

examples.text: A group of 100 people selected from 500+ applicants to participate in a 90-day sprint for starting a school community received Hormozi's 13 rules. By day 60 of the Rule of 100, practitioners reported having more business than they could handle; those who tagged Hormozi on day 4, 20, and 30 (early checkpoint-seekers) had not yet experienced the compounding effect visible by day 60.

Milo Sarychev, a bodybuilding coach, teaches that finding physical pain during training and staying within it (rather than avoiding it) forces muscular adaptation and growth; the pain is the signal of the stimulus that creates change.

Hormozi's own early experience: sleeping on the floor while running his first gym, so exhausted that good sleep could not repair the fatigue. The specific experiences have largely faded from memory, but he retains the narrative (the words he told himself) more vividly than the suffering itself.

practices.text: Google first when encountering something you don't know how to do; if you figure it out, post the solution because others likely struggled with the same thing.
Execute the Rule of 100 daily: reach out to 100 people, spend 100 minutes creating content, spend $100+ on ads, and spend 100 minutes improving ads and researching ad performance.
Prepare mentally for week two, when initial excitement ends and the work becomes a grind; this is the true test of commitment.
Lean into pain during repetitive work rather than avoiding it; use pain as a signal to seek improvement and develop better methods.
Never complain; redirect energy spent on complaints into problem-solving and improvement.
When claiming a tactic or channel doesn't work, immediately reframe as 'I haven't learned to make it work yet' or 'I'm not skilled enough at it yet.'
